description: Why the wartime alliance collapsed, the arms race, Berlin, Cuba and the Soviet-Afghan War.
content_html:
From Alliance to Cold War

The alliance between the Soviet Union, the United States and Britain that defeated Hitler began to fracture almost as soon as the war ended. Deep ideological differences between communism and Western capitalism had never really disappeared; wartime cooperation had been driven by a common enemy, not shared values. By 1947, the wartime coalition had collapsed into the prolonged standoff known as the Cold War.

Key turning points included the Soviet refusal to allow free elections in Eastern Europe, the announcement of the Truman Doctrine in 1947 (committing the USA to containing communism), and Winston Churchill's famous “Iron Curtain” speech in Fulton, Missouri in March 1946. Stalin's establishment of Soviet-backed communist governments across Eastern Europe created what Churchill described as an “iron curtain” dividing the continent.

Key Fact

The Cold War emerged from the breakdown of the wartime alliance between 1945 and 1947. Key markers include Churchill’s “Iron Curtain” speech (March 1946) and the Truman Doctrine (March 1947). By 1947 Europe was divided into Soviet-aligned East and American-aligned West.

The Warsaw Pact and NATO

In 1949, the Western powers formed NATO (the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation) — a military alliance committing members to collective defence. In direct response, the Soviet Union formed the Warsaw Pact in 1955. The formation of two competing military blocs institutionalised the division of Europe.

The USSR demonstrated its willingness to use force to maintain control of its satellite states when Hungary attempted to leave the Warsaw Pact in 1956. Soviet tanks crushed the Hungarian uprising, killing thousands and confirming that Eastern European states had no genuine independence. A similar intervention suppressed the Prague Spring in Czechoslovakia in 1968. After the Prague Spring, Brezhnev Doctrine explicitly justified intervention in any socialist country threatened by counter-revolution.

At the heart of the Cold War was the nuclear arms race. The USA had used atomic bombs against Japan in 1945; the Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb in 1949 and its first hydrogen bomb in 1953. Both sides built up arsenals capable of destroying human civilisation many times over. This mutual vulnerability created a doctrine of MAD (Mutually Assured Destruction) that, paradoxically, made direct war less likely.

The Space Race ran alongside the arms race: the USSR launched the world's first artificial satellite, Sputnik, in October 1957, shocking the Western world. Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space in April 1961. The USA responded with massive investment in NASA, eventually landing on the Moon in 1969. The Space Race had genuine scientific importance but was also a propaganda contest, with each side using achievements in space to demonstrate the superiority of their system.

Hot Spots: Berlin and Cuba

Berlin — divided between East and West since 1945 but located entirely within Soviet-controlled East Germany — was the most dangerous flashpoint of the early Cold War. From 1949 to 1961, roughly three million East Germans fled to the West through Berlin. In August 1961 East Germany, with Soviet backing, began construction of the Berlin Wall, sealing the border. The Wall remained until November 1989.

The most dangerous moment of the Cold War came during the Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962. American U-2 spy planes discovered Soviet nuclear missiles being installed in Cuba, just 90 miles from Florida. For thirteen days US President Kennedy and Soviet leader Khrushchev stood at the brink of nuclear war. The crisis was resolved when the Soviets agreed to remove the missiles in exchange for American pledges not to invade Cuba and a secret agreement to remove American missiles from Turkey. The crisis led both sides to establish a direct communication hotline between Washington and Moscow.

Key Fact

The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 was the closest the Cold War came to nuclear conflict. It was resolved when the Soviets withdrew missiles from Cuba in exchange for US guarantees not to invade Cuba and a secret agreement to remove American missiles from Turkey.

In December 1979 the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan to support a struggling communist government. The war quickly became a costly quagmire: Soviet forces controlled the cities but could not pacify the countryside against the American-backed mujahideen guerrilla fighters. The war lasted nine years, killing approximately 15,000 Soviet soldiers and vast numbers of Afghans, and contributing significantly to Soviet economic strain.

The invasion revived Cold War tensions after the relative relaxation of détente in the 1970s. US President Reagan accelerated American defence spending dramatically from 1981, pursuing his Strategic Defense Initiative (“Star Wars”) and announcing that the USSR was an “evil empire.” This “Second Cold War” placed enormous economic pressure on a Soviet system already struggling with stagnation. Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan was finally completed in February 1989 under Gorbachev.
exam_tip_html: For questions on Cold War tensions, be careful to explain why specific events increased or decreased tension — don’t just describe what happened. For ‘Explain a Cause’ or ‘Explain a Consequence’ questions about the Cold War, precise dates and named events (Truman Doctrine 1947, Warsaw Pact 1955, Cuban Missile Crisis 1962, Afghan invasion 1979) will lift your answer. For 16-mark Period Essays, remember you must reach a substantiated overall judgement, not just provide a balanced narrative.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Cold War emerged 1945–47 from ideological differences; the Warsaw Pact (1955) and NATO divided Europe into two military blocs. The Brezhnev Doctrine (1968) stated the USSR would intervene in any socialist country under threat.
  • Key flashpoints: the Berlin Wall (built 1961) sealed the Iron Curtain; the Cuban Missile Crisis (October 1962) brought the world to the brink of nuclear war.
  • The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 triggered the “Second Cold War”, with Reagan massively increasing US defence spending; the economic strain contributed to Soviet decline.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Warsaw Pact, established in 1955.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 2 marks. Candidates may refer to: it was a Soviet-led military alliance of Eastern European communist states; it was formed as a direct response to NATO; members were required to support each other militarily; it gave the USSR formal military leadership over Eastern European states.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: clear feature with developed explanation.
Secure: feature identified with basic explanation.
Developing: feature stated but not developed.
Emerging: vague or incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for development). Candidates may include: the USA discovered Soviet nuclear missiles being installed in Cuba in October 1962; President Kennedy and Khrushchev faced a 13-day stand-off; the crisis was resolved with Soviet withdrawal of missiles in exchange for US pledges not to invade Cuba; a direct communication hotline was established between Washington and Moscow afterwards.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: two features both fully developed.
Secure: two features, at least one developed.
Developing: two features identified but neither developed.
Emerging: only one feature, or no development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the collapse of the wartime alliance between the Soviet Union and the Western powers after 1945.
practice_questions.marks:
Candidates should identify a cause and explain why it led to the breakdown. Key causes: ideological differences between communism and capitalism that had always existed; Soviet expansion in Eastern Europe and refusal to allow free elections; the Truman Doctrine (1947) which committed the USA to containing communism.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: precise cause, causal chain explained, specific knowledge.
Secure: cause identified and explained with relevant knowledge.
Developing: cause identified but explanation is descriptive.
Emerging: simple point with no causal reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 for Cold War relations.
practice_questions.marks:
Top-band answers address significance at the time AND over time. At the time: ended the era of détente; triggered US boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympics; led to American support for mujahideen fighters. Over time: the nine-year war killed approximately 15,000 Soviet soldiers, damaged Soviet prestige, strained the economy and contributed to the conditions that produced Gorbachev's reforms and ultimately Soviet collapse.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: significance at time and over time, precise knowledge, sustained analysis.
Secure: significance in two ways, relevant knowledge.
Developing: significance at one point.
Emerging: description without significance judgement.

practice_questions.text:
The following is an interpretation of Cold War tensions:

“The Soviet Union was more responsible than the United States for causing and prolonging the Cold War.”

How far do you agree with this interpretation? Use your knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Candidates must agree AND disagree and reach a substantiated judgement.

Agreement: Soviet refusal to allow free elections in Eastern Europe broke wartime agreements; formation of Soviet satellite states created the Iron Curtain; the Berlin Wall was built to prevent emigration; the Brezhnev Doctrine justified Soviet intervention in sovereign states; invasion of Afghanistan was unprovoked aggression.

Disagreement: the Truman Doctrine of 1947 committed the USA to global anti-communism; the Marshall Plan excluded Eastern Europe, deepening division; Reagan's 'Second Cold War' military build-up was provocative; American nuclear monopoly (1945-49) forced Soviet nuclear development.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: balanced argument, precise evidence, substantiated conclusion.
Secure: both sides covered, conclusion reached.
Developing: one-sided or conclusion absent.
Emerging: descriptive, no analytical engagement.

practice_questions.text: How far did Cold War tensions change between 1945 and 1991? Use your knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band requires a substantiated overall judgement weighing change against continuity.

Change: from open confrontation (Berlin Blockade 1948) to arms control treaties (SALT I 1972); détente in the 1970s; Gorbachev's ending of the Cold War in the late 1980s.

Continuity: nuclear threat remained throughout; proxy conflicts continued (Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan); ideological competition never fully ended until 1991.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: sustained argument weighing change and continuity, clear judgement.
Secure: two or more factors or periods explained, conclusion reached.
Developing: factors listed, limited weighing.
Emerging: one factor or descriptive throughout.

glossary_terms.definition: The state of geopolitical tension between the Soviet Union and the United States from roughly 1947 to 1991, fought through proxies, propaganda and the arms race rather than direct military conflict.
President Truman's 1947 policy committing the United States to containing the spread of communism worldwide.
The Soviet-led military alliance of Eastern European communist states established in 1955 as a counterpart to NATO.
The Soviet doctrine announced in 1968 stating the USSR reserved the right to intervene in any socialist country where socialism was under threat.
The barrier built by East Germany from August 1961, dividing East and West Berlin and becoming the most potent symbol of the Iron Curtain.
Mutually Assured Destruction: the Cold War logic that any nuclear first strike would trigger a devastating retaliatory strike, making nuclear war irrational for both sides.
The policy of easing Cold War tensions through diplomacy, trade agreements and arms control treaties, pursued by both superpowers from the late 1960s to the late 1970s.
